column4: The deniers use ضَلَلْنَا فِي الْأَرْضِ for bodies lost into earth and immediately reject a “new creation,” directly joining the section’s burial sense of the ض ل ل family to re-creation.
God’s answer names the whole movement: creation from earth, return into it, and another bringing-out, تَارَةً أُخْرَىٰ; this is the section’s funeral-to-second-creation arc in one ayah.
The crow scratches the earth to show Cain how to conceal his brother’s corpse, staging the section’s act of putting the dead into the ground.
ثُمَّ أَمَاتَهُ فَأَقْبَرَهُ places death and burial in immediate sequence, making literal the funeral background heard in the source roots.
After 80:21’s burial, ثُمَّ إِذَا شَاءَ أَنْشَرَهُ moves from the grave to being raised, completing exactly the section’s directional sequence.
Life on earth, death in it, and emergence from it are stated as one cycle; the earth is both place of burial and point of renewed appearance.
Human creation is pictured as growth from the earth, beginning the same earthward and earth-outward movement that the section develops.
ثُمَّ يُعِيدُكُمْ فِيهَا وَيُخْرِجُكُمْ إِخْرَاجًا explicitly returns people to earth and brings them out, completing 71:17’s creation image as burial and resurrection.
The earth is called كِفَاتًا, a containing place; the next ayah specifies that it gathers both living and dead, closely matching the section’s lodging and burial places.
أَحْيَاءً وَأَمْوَاتًا makes the earth of 77:25 a receptacle for living and dead together, a compact boundary between dwelling and grave.
The prohibition on praying over a dead person and standing at his grave stages the funeral rite and graveside directly.
The ayah runs from earthen origin through womb stages and death, then revives dead earth as evidence for renewed human life; it develops both halves of the section’s passage.
Following the creation and dead-earth demonstration, the ayah states that God gives life to the dead, identifying the transition displayed in 22:5.
The coming Hour culminates in God raising those in the graves, turning burial into renewed presence.
A man is made dead for a hundred years, raised, and shown bones assembled and clothed with flesh; the corpse-to-recreated-body movement is displayed rather than merely asserted.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay, opening a sequence that proceeds through womb, death, and resurrection in 23:13–16.
The drop is placed in قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ, a secure lodging; this supplies a life-side counterpart to the section’s grave and depository language.
After successive formations God produces خَلْقًا آخَرَ, an “other creation”; within 23:12–16 it anticipates the later passage from death to raising.
ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ لَمَيِّتُونَ places death after the first formation and before the next ayah’s resurrection.
ثُمَّ إِنَّكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ تُبْعَثُونَ completes 23:12–15’s ordered movement from earth and gestation through death to renewed life.
At the trumpet blast people hasten from the graves, a direct scene of the buried becoming present again.
Those newly raised ask who awakened them from their resting place; their speech preserves the grave-as-resting-place image while recognizing resurrection.
The objection “when we have died and become dust” calls bodily return remote, voicing the same denial that the section answers through burial and new creation.
God knows what the earth diminishes of the dead and has a preserving record, directly answering 50:3’s fear that burial makes the body irretrievably lost.
The earth splits away from people as they emerge rapidly; burial ground itself opens into resurrection.
People come out of the graves like scattered locusts, giving the section’s movement out of burial a vivid collective scene.
They emerge rapidly from graves as if racing toward a marker, an explicit reversal of emplacement in the grave.
وَإِذَا الْقُبُورُ بُعْثِرَتْ makes the graves themselves overturned and emptied, exposing what burial had covered.
The ayah asks about the moment when what is in the graves is scattered out, directly moving hidden corpses into disclosure.
The earth casts out its burdens; in the resurrection sequence, what had been deposited in it is brought forth.
The resurrecting earth then تُحَدِّثُ أَخْبَارَهَا, joining the source section’s ح د ث “tell/come to be” root to a scene where the buried have just emerged.
The human being doubts that God will gather his bones, reducing the resurrection objection to the dispersed remains of a corpse.
God answers that even the fingertips can be proportioned again, making renewed embodiment more exact than merely collecting bones.
The deniers ask whether they will be returned to the former state, posing renewal as a reversal back into life.
Their question about decayed bones gives the bodily and funerary substance of the “return” in 79:10.
A single blast is the act that reverses the condition of the decayed bones in 79:11.
After that blast they are suddenly upon the earth’s surface, completing movement from buried remains to visible presence.
The deniers ask whether death, dust, and bones can end in being raised, directly staging the section’s burial-to-creation question.
They add their “first forefathers,” extending the question from one corpse to generations already buried.
The answer “yes” reverses the denial of 37:16–17 and says they will return humbled.
The objection joins death, dust, bones, and resurrection in the same order as the section’s passage from burial language to renewed existence.
Mention of the first forefathers makes long-buried generations part of 56:47’s objection.
The reply gathers الْأَوَّلِينَ وَالْآخِرِينَ, using the first/later polarity central to the section’s reading of creation.
All those generations are gathered at an appointed time, answering the dispersed dust and bones of 56:47.
Bones and crumbled remains are set against خَلْقًا جَدِيدًا, another direct formulation of the section’s corpse-to-new-creation transition.
The answer identifies the restorer as the One who originated them أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ, making first creation the warrant for return.
God’s call receives their response and brings them out of their former condition, completing the answer begun in 17:51.
The human being asks whether, after dying, he will be brought out alive; the wording directly crosses death, emergence, and life.
The reply recalls that God created the human being before when he was nothing, exactly matching the source’s “being after non-being” sense.
The objection puts becoming dust beside being in a new creation, directly matching the section’s burial and re-existence pairing.
Death, dust, bones, and being raised are again placed in one skeptical question, a close parallel to the objection quoted in the section.
The disbelievers ask whether they and their fathers will be brought out after becoming dust, making emergence from ancestral burial explicit.
The mock announcement links complete bodily disintegration to خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ, the same apparent gap between corpse and renewed existence.
A man displays decayed bones and asks who can revive them, turning the denial into a visible corpse-remains scene.
The answer names the One who produced the bones أَوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ; first origination guarantees their revival.
The deniers call death only مَوْتَتُنَا الْأُولَىٰ and deny being raised, bringing the “first” root into the death-versus-second-life dispute.
The claim that people merely die and live and that time destroys them voices the denial of any passage beyond worldly succession.
God’s answer orders life, death, and gathering on the Resurrection Day, correcting 45:24’s attempt to close the sequence at death.
A child rejects his parents’ promise that he will be brought out after generations have passed, combining family farewell, ancestral death, and resurrection denial.
Those who claim they will never be raised receive a direct divine oath that they will be raised and told what they did.
The emphatic oath that God will not raise whoever dies is answered as a binding promise, making the denial and answer explicit in one ayah.
When resurrection after death is announced, the disbelievers dismiss it as magic; this is another clearly marked version of the section’s objection scene.
The denial “only our worldly life” and “we will not be raised” states the boundary the section’s movement beyond death crosses.
A messenger’s opponents ridicule the promise that after death, dust, and bones they will be brought out.
Their counterclaim restricts existence to worldly dying and living and denies being raised, clarifying the resistance voiced in 23:35.
The command to observe how creation began culminates in النَّشْأَةَ الْآخِرَةَ, directly naming the “later/second creation” sense highlighted in the source.
وَأَنَّ عَلَيْهِ النَّشْأَةَ الْأُخْرَىٰ states that the other creation belongs to God, an exact Qur’anic realization of the section’s gloss of the ء خ ر family.
God’s ordaining of death opens a sequence about replacement and a form of creation not yet known.
God can replace people and produce them in a form they do not know, supplying the renewed-existence side of 56:60’s death.
Knowledge of النَّشْأَةَ الْأُولَىٰ is invoked as evidence for the post-death transformation in 56:60–61, pairing first creation with another.
As creation began أَوَّلَ خَلْقٍ, God will repeat it; the image of rolling the sky also places first origination and re-creation in one promise.
Failure is denied in الْخَلْقِ الْأَوَّلِ, while the deniers remain confused about خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ; first and renewed creation are explicitly paired.
God reminds Zechariah, “I created you before when you were nothing,” stating the source’s definition of existence after nonexistence almost exactly.
Humanity once was not a thing mentioned, supplying the “before it existed” half of the source’s explanation of coming into being.
Two orphan boys are named together with their righteous father and the inheritance hidden for them; the context makes the absent father behind يَتِيم visible.
At death a person asks to be sent back, staging the moment when farewell becomes irreversible.
A barrier stands behind the dead until the day they are raised, locating burial-time between departure and renewed existence.
The stupor of death arrives with truth, presenting the actual threshold that the section’s farewell vocabulary surrounds.
The trumpet follows the death-threshold in 50:19 and announces the threatened day, moving immediately from dying to resurrection.
Life reaching the collarbones stages the physical onset of death and the beginning of final farewell.
The dying person realizes أَنَّهُ الْفِرَاقُ, “that it is the parting,” making the section’s farewell-to-the-dead sense explicit.
The dying person’s course is then toward the Lord, carrying the deathbed parting into the encounter denied in 32:10.
The soul reaching the throat presents the same deathbed boundary as 75:26 in the presence of those saying farewell.
The witnesses are challenged to return the departing soul if they are beyond judgment; their inability marks death’s one-way boundary before resurrection.
God takes souls at death and in sleep, retaining the one sentenced to death and releasing the other; it distinguishes temporary covering/rest from final departure.
The angel of death takes people and they are then returned to their Lord, spelling out the meeting whose denial closes 32:10.
Death and life are themselves created in an ordered test, so death is a made stage rather than the end of existence.
Abraham names God as the One who causes him to die and then gives him life, a personal confession of the section’s movement.
Creation from dust and a drop proceeds through life stages to death, tracing existence from nonbeing toward the funeral threshold.
The One who gives life and death brings a thing into being by saying “Be”; this joins death-to-life with the source’s “made existent after not existing” gloss.
People were lifeless, were given life, will be made to die and given life again, then returned to God; the whole sequence is explicit.
A slain person is restored to life as a displayed sign that God gives life to the dead.
A multitude fleeing death are made to die and then revived, turning death and renewed life into a collective enacted scene.
Abraham is shown how dead birds are restored and summoned, making reassembly and renewed motion perceptible.
After the thunderbolt death, the people are raised so that they may give thanks; the ayah explicitly reverses death.
Jesus’ sign of giving life to the dead by God’s permission enacts the same passage from corpse to life within worldly time.
God recalls Jesus bringing the dead out alive by divine permission, repeating the concrete death-to-life sign.
Rain revives a dead land and the ayah says “thus We bring out the dead,” making earth’s greening a direct analogue for emergence from burial.
Rain revives dead land and the ayah explicitly identifies that scene with النُّشُورُ, resurrection.
The lifeless earth stirs and grows with water, and its reviver is declared able to give life to the dead.
Measured water revives a dead land and “thus you will be brought out,” connecting emergence from earth to resurrection.
Bringing living from dead and dead from living is joined to reviving earth and “thus you are brought out,” a precise transition across the boundary.
The effects of mercy revive earth after death, then the same Giver is named as the One who revives the dead.
Origin from one soul is followed by مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمُسْتَوْدَعٌ, the stable and entrusted places that the source reads across life, death, and return.
وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ closely echoes 93:4 while making the “later” realm enduring, grounding the source’s move from first life toward what follows it.
Moses is put alive as an infant into التَّابُوتِ and cast on the water; the coffin-shaped chest carries vulnerable life toward rescue rather than a corpse toward burial.
The living child from the chest is returned to his mother so that she may cease grieving, completing the reversal of funeral farewell begun in 20:39.
التَّابُوتُ is carried by angels and contains tranquility and family relics; this carried chest bears a sign and inherited remains rather than a dead body.
Those killed in God’s path must not be called dead but living, setting a revealed boundary against judging life solely from the corpse and funeral.
The slain are described as alive and provided for with their Lord, reversing the apparent finality of their deaths.

A person described as dead is given life and a light to walk by; physical death-and-revival language is redirected to guidance, just as the source hears funeral language without forcing it onto 93’s surface meaning.
The living and dead are not equal, and those in graves cannot be made to hear; the grave here marks the boundary of prophetic address rather than the later raising.
The sleepers are disclosed so people may know the resurrection promise is true, and the debate about building over them gives their resting place the aspect of a tomb.
Every creature’s provision is known together with its مُسْتَقَرّ and مُسْتَوْدَع; the same two-place vocabulary as 6:98 extends the image across creaturely lodging and deposit.
Within the orphan-property passage, people are told to fear leaving weak offspring behind; it makes the parental death presupposed by orphanhood visible.
At the deathbed people ask who might heal or save the dying person, continuing the farewell scene between the collarbones and recognized parting.
One leg is wound with the other as death closes over the body, supplying the bodily middle of 75:26–30’s departure scene.
Those around the dying person look on, making 56:83’s soul-at-the-throat moment a witnessed farewell.
God is nearer to the dying person than the witnesses can see, adding unseen divine presence to the human farewell scene.
Divine messengers take a person at death without neglect, presenting death as a transfer under custody rather than disappearance.
After being taken in death, people are returned to God for judgment, completing the transfer begun in 6:61.
Angels take the good at death with a greeting of peace and entry into the Garden, turning the final farewell into a welcome elsewhere.
Every soul tastes death and receives full recompense on Resurrection Day, placing death before rather than after the final outcome.
Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, stating the universal departure and return that frame the image.
Every soul tastes death and is then returned to God, repeating the same death-to-return order in the context of migration and worship.
God brings the living out of the dead and the dead out of the living, a compact reciprocal formulation of the boundary crossed by the section.
The splitting of seed and kernel is joined to bringing living from dead and dead from living, giving the transition a buried-seed analogue.
The opponents acknowledge that God brings living from dead and dead from living, so their own answer supplies a premise for renewed life.
Water gives life to earth after its death; although resurrection is not stated in this ayah, the visible earthward transition concretely parallels the image.
The declaration that God revives earth after its death supplies a concise natural analogue for life after burial.
Dead earth is revived and grain is brought out from it, offering emergence of life from buried ground as a sign alongside the later bone-resurrection argument.
God gives life and causes death, and to Him people return; the return prevents death from closing the sequence.
God gives life, causes death, and then gives life again, a compact statement of the section’s direction.
“We give life and cause death, and to Us is the destination” joins mortality to an onward return in the resurrection passage.
At judgment people find وَجَدُوا what they did made present, حَاضِرًا; the source root of “finding/existence” thus meets post-death disclosure rather than creation itself.
The question whether people were created from nothing or are creators presses the source’s concern with how what was not comes to be, though it does not itself stage burial.
لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ أَمْرًا uses the source’s ح د ث family for God bringing about a new state after the former one, a non-funerary but relevant sense of coming-to-be.
God makes night a covering, sleep a repose, and day a rising; the ayah joins the source’s night-cover image to a daily analogue of death and resurrection.
The testament rule explicitly joins travel on the earth with the calamity of death, bringing together the living traveler and the dying person behind the source’s two uses of farewell.
When death comes to Jacob, he addresses his sons about what they will worship after him; this is an actual deathbed farewell spoken by the departing to the living.
In the throes of death the wrongdoers are ordered by the angels to yield their souls, staging the final separation and its unseen witnesses.
The trumpet causes all in the heavens and earth to die, then a second blast leaves them standing and looking; death and renewed embodied presence are shown in immediate succession.
At judgment people confess two deaths and two lives, explicitly recognizing repeated passage across the life-death boundary they had denied.
Peace attends John on the day of birth, the day of death, and the day he is raised alive, placing a whole human course in the section’s order.
Jesus names his birth, death, and being raised alive as three marked days, repeating the same life-to-death-to-life sequence in first-person speech.
People come to God alone “as We created you the first time” and leave their former gifts behind; return is measured against first creation and worldly farewell.
Those presented before God are told that they have come as they were created the first time, making resurrection a return to first origination.
Return to God is grounded in His beginning creation and repeating it, a direct formulation of first and renewed existence.
The question asks who begins creation and then repeats it, and the answer names God; repeated creation is used against the deniers’ false objects of worship.
Beginning creation and repeating it are posed as a challenge about divine identity, making renewed origination the decisive act.
God begins creation, repeats it, and then people are returned to Him, stating the full direction in one ayah.
The One who begins creation repeats it; the repeated formula directly supports the source’s reading of a later creation after the first.
إِنَّهُ هُوَ يُبْدِئُ وَيُعِيدُ compresses first origination and return into paired divine acts.
The creation and resurrection of all people are said to be like those of a single soul, explicitly joining the two creative acts.
Creation of the heavens and earth is invoked as proof that God can give life to the dead, answering resurrection denial with prior creation.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is able to create people’s like, continuing the answer to the decayed-bones objection.
A thing exists when God wills it and says “Be”; after the bone-resurrection argument, this states the source’s coming-into-being sense as the mechanism of the answer.
Following the denied promise to raise the dead, God’s word to a willed thing is simply that it be, and it is; existence after nonexistence answers the denial.
The Creator of heaven and earth says “Be” and it is, while the same ayah names the day of the trumpet; first creation and eschatological reappearance meet in one statement.
The human being was a drop of emitted fluid, beginning the first-creation proof that culminates in reviving the dead.
The drop becomes a clinging form which God creates and proportions, displaying formation from an earlier unformed state.
The completed first-creation account ends by asking whether its Creator can give life to the dead, making the inference explicit.
The command that the human consider what he was created from opens a first-origination proof of his return.
Creation from an emitted fluid supplies the material starting point of the return argument.
The fluid’s emergence from within the body completes the first-formation detail on which the following claim of return rests.
God is declared able to return the human being, turning the remembered first origin of 86:5–7 toward renewed existence.
“We created you” confronts disbelief just before the passage moves through procreation, death, replacement, and first creation.
Emitted seed is presented as the material beginning of a life that the passage later carries through death and another formation.
The question whether humans create that seed or God does makes divine origination the premise for the following death-and-replacement sequence.
God causes death and gives life, immediately before the passage’s statement of the other creation.
The death from which people flee will meet them, after which they are returned to the Knower; attempted avoidance ends in departure and return.
The defrauders are asked whether they think they will be raised, directing moral forgetfulness to renewed existence.
Their raising is assigned to a tremendous day, specifying the time implied by 83:4.
On that day humanity stands before the Lord of the worlds, supplying the bodily presence and meeting produced by the raising.
After emergence from the graves, one cry leaves everyone brought present before God, completing 36:51–52’s scene.
The earth casts out what is within it and becomes empty; in the judgment sequence this pictures the buried released from their repository.
God raises the sleepers after their long enclosed sleep, beginning the episode that 18:21 explicitly makes evidence for resurrection.
“Thus We raised them” brings the sleepers back into speech and movement after their deathlike interval, a lived analogue of renewed existence.
God takes people during the night and raises them during the day until the fixed term; daily sleep and waking form a reversible counterpart to death and final raising.
The deniers demand that their fathers be brought back, making ancestral death the test they set against resurrection.
The opponents’ sole argument is the challenge to bring their fathers, turning the buried previous generation into their demanded proof.
A remembered skeptic had asked whether death, dust, and bones could end in judgment; the question is recalled from within the afterlife that answers it.
The answer tells deniers to imagine themselves stone or iron, showing that even a form they think resistant to decay cannot block the Creator’s return.
Those who denied raising in 6:29 are made to stand before their Lord and acknowledge its truth, completing objection with encounter.
A man has been killed and the killers conceal the act; this supplies the actual corpse whose revival follows in 2:73.
The thunderbolt takes the people while they look on, supplying the death that 2:56 then reverses by raising them.
Creation from a lowly fluid begins a passage that moves through a secure lodging and then the earth’s containment of living and dead.
The fluid is placed in قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ, a secure repository that forms a life-side counterpart to the earth as container in 77:25–26.
The womb-deposit remains until a known measure, distinguishing its timed custody from the later custody of the dead in earth.
When the meeting denied in 32:10 occurs, the guilty stand before their Lord and ask to be returned, showing the promised emergence and its irreversible direction.
The buried-alive girl is made present and questioned; unlike ordinary burial after death, this grave was used to kill a living child.
The question “for what sin was she killed?” exposes the living burial of 81:8 as murder, sharply reversing the proper order of death and interment.
The ashamed father considers hiding his living daughter in the dust, turning burial from care for a corpse into an act against life.
The sleepers look awake although asleep and their bodies are turned, holding visible signs of life and deathlike repose together during their long enclosure.
The one entering Hell neither dies there nor lives, a suspended boundary that reverses the section’s directional passage from death into renewed life.
In the great Fire a person neither dies nor lives, repeating the exceptional state in which the normal death-life sequence is withheld.
Death comes at the condemned person from every side yet he does not die, a punitive refusal of the release ordinarily marked by death.
The condemned are neither finished by death nor relieved, extending life without the death-and-return transition developed in the section.
False gods are themselves created and possess neither death, life, nor resurrection; their incapacity sets a boundary around acts that belong to the Creator.
The invoked beings are “dead, not living” and do not know when they will be raised, applying death-and-resurrection language to powerless objects of worship.
The king claims “I give life and cause death,” but Abraham’s challenge exposes this as a counterfeit use of the acts the section attributes to God.
At death the messengers take the wrongdoers and question them about what they invoked, presenting death as custody followed by interrogation.
Angels take the disbelievers at death while striking them, another concrete form of the soul’s forced departure.
Angels take the souls of wrongdoers, who then offer submission; it forms the adverse counterpart to the peaceful taking in 16:32.
Angels take the disbelievers while striking faces and backs, continuing the Qur’anic scenes of death as an enacted transfer.
The tranquil soul is addressed directly, opening a farewell that becomes a summons to return.
The soul is told to return to its Lord, satisfied and accepted, turning departure from the former life into arrival.
Entry among God’s servants gives the returning soul a new company after its individual farewell.
Entry into Paradise completes the sequence as welcome into another abode.
God gives life, causes death, and remains the inheritor, placing creaturely mortality inside continuing divine possession.
God gives life and causes death; the accompanying alternation of night and day adds a recurring visible cycle to the claim.
God gives life and causes death and is Lord of the hearers and their first fathers, joining mortality to the generations invoked by deniers.
The One who owns the heavens and earth gives life and causes death, identifying both thresholds as divine acts.
A drop when emitted supplies the first-creation detail between God’s giving life and death in 53:44 and the other creation in 53:47.
The Originator brings a decreed thing into being by saying “Be”; this is a cosmic formulation of existence after nonexistence, though burial is not in view.
The Creator of the heavens and earth is said able to create people’s like and to have set a term for them, a later reprise of the answer to 17:49’s denial.
Earth is assigned as a temporary dwelling and provision until a term, establishing the living side of the earth-cycle completed by death and emergence in 7:25.
On the resurrection day the settled destination is to the Lord, giving the “resting place” vocabulary an eschatological endpoint rather than a grave.
“Far, far is what you are promised” records the opponents’ scornful stance toward the promised emergence described in 23:35.
The deniers say that they and their fathers were promised this before, adding generational memory to their dust-and-bones objection in 23:82.
The complaint that they and their fathers had long been promised resurrection continues 27:67’s image of ancestral dust.
The deniers call the proposed return a losing one, preserving their dismissive stance between the decayed-bones question and the trumpet’s answer.
Formation as male and female completes the first bodily creation recalled before 75:40 draws the inference to reviving the dead.
The companions’ hearing is sealed in the cave for years, beginning the enclosed, deathlike sleep from which 18:12 raises them.
The unresponsive are set beside “the dead,” whom God will raise and return; the ayah pivots from a figurative deafness to literal resurrection.
The thirsty person “finds” the mirage to be nothing and then finds God there for reckoning; the source’s و ج د family here turns on absent versus encountered reality in an afterlife-facing image.
